work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: In illud: Quando ipsi subiciet omnia

paragraphs.text: Yesterday, brothers, we preached on the endless kingdom of Christ. Our sermon came when your attention was at its height, and it gave the hearers sufficient proof. I call it sufficient, not as measured against the dignity of what is preached, but as measured against the ability of the preacher. For there is nothing on earth or in heaven that can worthily praise the much-praised dignity of the Only-begotten. The prophets proclaimed many things beforehand about the Lord's divine appearing; the law decreed many things; the apostles preached many things; the evangelists told many things; and none of them has been able to reach his dignity. If so many rivers of the Holy Spirit, with their ever-flowing and pure streams, exhausted all human power and still uttered nothing worthy of the divine power, where will the tiniest drop of speech show itself, when a subject of such dignity lies before it? A mortal tongue cannot worthily praise an immortal nature; human speech cannot worthily praise the world-making Word of God. What then? We preach as much as we are able, since we are not equal to as much as we ought. In other contests it is the victors who carry off the crowns, but in the labors of theology it is those who confess themselves defeated who carry off the crowns of right-mindedness. So let us be defeated by speaking, rather than be condemned for keeping silent.

Someone will say that the endlessness of the kingdom has been shown, in that he hands over the kingdom to God the Father: that is, the world, once ruled by sin and later ruled by grace. But the words "When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him" have been left unexamined. So it is necessary to say what we can, lest our silence lay a stumbling block for the ill-minded. You must all know, brothers, that we did not leave this out on purpose. We had delivered our argument as complete and thoroughly examined, and we thought that what remained had already been made clear by what came before. For one aim and one argument both resolves what came before and clarifies what lies before us: the apostle said these things by way of accommodation. There, the handing over of the kingdom to God the Father does not accord with the power of the proclamation. The expression is introduced only on the surface, because of the weakness of those who had been brought up out of the error of many gods ("I gave you milk to drink, not solid food"). In the same way, and for the same reason, this too is said now. Everywhere the apostle's aim is to show that the divine nature is never at variance with itself, and that the Son does not oppose the Father, as the impious notion of the Jews had it. For they said, "This man is not from God, because he does not keep the sabbath." So he presents one nature free of discord, one concord, one word, one will, one authority, one God in all, to cut away the shoots of the error of many gods. As the diligent among you will remember, we showed that the same passage that bears witness to the dignity of the Father proclaims the dignity of Christ in the very same words and syllables. Just as it says there, "that God may be all in all," so it says of the Only-begotten, "but Christ is all and in all." What then does "will be subjected" mean? He is preparing a remedy for the pagan disease. He is not introducing a doctrine of the Church; he is driving out a pagan notion. But if we must speak in absolute terms, he is speaking of a subjection of Christ that comes about through the Church. For when the Church is subjected, having nothing spurious or counterfeit, but offering God a sincere and genuine disposition, then he will truly be subjected to him.

"That is a forced reading," he says, "and not enough to persuade the ill-minded." Then so that you may learn that whatever things of this kind are ascribed to Christ are seen in the Church of Christ, I will bring before you the Master of the Church himself as witness. But let me begin a little further back, so that what I say may be clear. While Christ was in this world in the flesh, fulfilling the human dispensation for the salvation of the world, the Savior of the world was persecuted by the Jews and hounded by the enemies of truth, and the source of all benefits was treated ungratefully by those who enjoyed them. But when he had fulfilled the whole dispensation through his passion, he passed over to the heavenly choirs, departing in body but filling all things in dignity. Taking up on high the body he had put on, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. He did not receive some foreign or alien glory; rather, he clothed the mortal body with that great dignity. After the ascension, then, and his release from suffering, after that much-praised resurrection and his removal into heaven, he was worshiped by the whole host above the heavens, with the whole bodyguard of angels standing about him. He was no longer among the afflicted, the persecuted or the hounded. Yet when he saw Paul raging against the Church and breathing great fury against the saints, he who after his passion was persecuted nowhere, but lived in such honor and divine glory, says to him: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" And yet I am not persecuting you, for you have the seat of honor in heaven. "Why are you persecuting me?" He makes the sufferings of the Church his own. "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" Do you see that the persecution of the Church is ascribed to Christ, the head of the Church? Just as he says that he himself is persecuted when the Church is persecuted, so here Paul says that Christ is subjected when the Church is subjected.

Take another proof of the argument as well: "For on the word of two or three witnesses every matter shall be established." This is not because the Master's voice needs further testimony. It is because, when Christ speaks, he is believed by the faithful, but his testimony does not convince unbelievers. We are not shoring up the Master's voice; we are silencing the ill-mindedness of the heretics. This Paul learned from Christ himself that persecution of the Church is referred to Christ. Knowing, then, that whatever the Church suffers is referred to Christ, he followed in the footsteps of the King's words and says somewhere in one of his letters: "I fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ." Is Christ, then, still afflicted after ascending into heaven? But see what follows: "I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ, for the sake of his body, which is the Church." Do you see how Christ makes both the sufferings and the honor of the Church his own? Have you honored the Church? You have honored Christ. Have you persecuted the Church? Even if not before his eyes, in your intention you have persecuted Christ. Think how great is the danger for those who grieve the Church, and how great the crown for those who honor it. "Whoever rejects you rejects me," says the Savior. I recognize that voice, O Master: it keeps to the Father's pattern. For the Father, too, said such things about his prophets of old, making outrages against the righteous his own. When Abimelech, king of the Philistines, took Sarah, the wife of Abraham, God said to him: "Give the man back his wife, for he is a prophet and will pray for you." In his defense he says: "Lord, I did not know that she was his wife; I did this with a pure heart." What then did God say to him? "I too knew that you did this with a pure heart; that is why I kept you from sinning against me." So it has been shown, brothers, that everything seen in the Church is referred to Christ. That is why the apostle says: "The Son" (that is, the Church) "will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him."

But the ill-minded man has another way out. "What?" he says. "Is the Church not subjected now, and will it only be subjected then, after the resurrection?" The same refutation answers your objection, heretic. Tell me: by your own argument, is Christ not subjected now? The words "When all things are subjected to him, then he will be subjected" would have had a point if he were not subjected at present. But if by your argument, heretic, he is always in subjection and never resists the Father, then "When all things are subjected to him, then he will be subjected" is superfluous. You cite countless texts to accuse him of subjection, and then you reserve a second subjection of his for some other time? If you hear Christ say, "I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me," at once you thrust out the horn of impiety and say, "Do you see how he is subject to the Father?" If you hear him say, "I do not speak on my own; the Father has given me a command, what to say and what to speak," at once you seize on the phrase and insist that Christ has no authority of his own but is subjected. If you hear him say, "I judge no one; there is one who seeks and judges," at once you snatch subjection out of the phrase. Since you show him to be subjected in all these texts, why do you bring forward an ill-minded supposition and say, "I follow the wording, not the sense: that he who is always subjected will be subjected then"? What, then, does the sense intend? Everywhere the apostle's aim is to abolish the error of many gods, to drive out the idea of discord from the nature that knows no discord, and to banish the suspicions of those who think wrongly. So he points to a subjection that is not forced, not compelled and not servile, but befits their concord in dignity.

But do not let anything said earlier take hold of you, brother, such as: "I do not speak this on my own; the Father has given me a command, what to say and what to speak." I fear that you may take what is said in the heat of combat against the heretics as the doctrine of the Church, and so set aside the sense of the preaching. On the former occasion our sermon, in defending the apostle's meaning, insisted that the apostles do not preach everything as doctrine, but put forward some things as doctrine and others by way of accommodation. In the same way I find that the very source of truth, the Master of the apostles and prophets, does not always speak as doctrine in keeping with his own dignity; at times he condescends, by way of accommodation, to the weakness of the people. Tell me, brother: when the Master of truth says, "If I bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true," shall I follow the wording? Shall I follow the bare expression? Shall I insult his dignity because of his accommodation? Even if I wanted to be ill-minded, the Master would not allow me. If I wrongly follow the wording, he will shut out my evil thought. He takes hold of my words as speaking otherwise of holy things, as carelessly confusing and insulting his dignity, and says: "Because I condescended to the Jews and said, 'If I bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true,' have you snatched up the phrase for blasphemy? Did you not hear me say elsewhere, 'Even if I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true'?" What then, brothers? Does the truth say things that contradict itself? Certainly not. But it speaks one way to those nurtured in the truth and another way to those cut off from the truth. It does not change itself; it adapts to people's dispositions. Why, then, does he say to the Jews, "I do not speak on my own; the Father has given me a command, what to say and what to speak"? Because they thought he was an enemy of the Mosaic law, giving commands contrary to the Father, who honored the sabbath through the law; and to outward appearance the new covenant seemed to be at odds with the old order. So, wishing to show that he was not at odds with God and was not preaching against the law, he says: "I do not speak on my own" (as you suspect), "but he himself has given me a command": he whom you worship. It is all but as if he were teaching them: "If you set these things aside, it is not my teaching you set aside; you are colliding with the God whom you yourselves confess." For suppose, brothers, that I took Christ's word so miserably, so humbly, so abjectly as to treat as the words of a servant the voice that says, "I do nothing on my own; the Father has given me commands, what to say and what to speak." Do you see what depths of impiety I fall into by thinking so? I make him not only lower than the Father but even less than the apostles. Listen to how. Paul says: "Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give my opinion." Paul speaks without a command, and Christ can say nothing on his own? "Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give my opinion." You allow Paul to give his opinion even without a command, yet you shut Christ up under the yoke of slavery and follow the wording that says, "I say nothing on my own"? And then, as I said before, he speaks one way to those nurtured in the truth and another to those cut off from it. Did the Jews suppose him to be the Son of God? Did the Jews have any notion of God the Word? Have you not heard what they say about him? "This man is not from God, because he does not keep the sabbath." They did not even suppose him to be a man of God; did they have any notion of the dignity of the Only-begotten? The same people said again about the Savior: "We know that this man is a sinner, because he does not keep the sabbath." Since they took him for a sinner and a man cut off from the truth, could they make room for his divinity at all, even in the faintest imagining?

So to people of that mind he lowered his voice. He taught them not to contradict the outward form that they thought was at variance with God's will, and said: "I do not speak on my own; he himself has given me a command, what to say and what to speak." But see how, with the sons of faith, he lays aside that submissive voice, puts on the authority of his divine dignity, and says: "You have heard that it was said to those of old, 'You shall not commit adultery': whoever looks at his neighbor's wife with desire has already sinned. But I say." Do you see how, where the hearer is faithful, the authority is plain, and where the hearer is suspicious, the teaching is shaped by accommodation?

Disturbance always springs up when the divine word is being heard. The devil, the enemy of souls, sees the word shooting sharpened arrows at his error, so he constantly troubles the hearers, hoping to escape the truth's refutation. A young man, Eutychus, disrupted Paul's teaching, and here too a young man has disrupted the people's listening, so as to test the hearers' resolve all the more. But let us, brothers, flee the tossing of the waves and bring our ship to anchor in the calm harbor of the truth. I do not want the digression to run on and get in the way of our subject.

Where the hearer is suspicious, the teaching is shaped by accommodation; where there is one truly nurtured in piety, the authority is plain. To the Jews he says, "I say nothing on my own"; to those of the household of faith, "You have heard that it was said to those of old, 'You shall not commit adultery.' But I say." The "I" shows the authority of the speaker. Everywhere, "I" bears witness to the authority of the one speaking, as when he says, "I am, I am, and even until you grow old, I am." And again he says to the Jews, "I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me." Today's reading from the Gospels resolves the difficulty raised by the heretics' notion. When the leper came to him, that man leprous in body but radiant in soul, he said to him: "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean." Look here for the heretics' rule. He ought then, to be consistent with his own words, to have said: "I do not will it; the Father wills it; be clean. For I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me. Did you not hear me say, 'I did not come to do my own will'?" If then, by the argument of the impious, you insist that his will is subject to another's authority, why do you ask for an act of authority from one who is subject to the Father's authority? But the Savior said none of this to the man who came to him in sincerity. He accepted the sincerity of his faith and gave him sincere and genuine salvation: "You came to me in faith; receive the remedy in faith. You credit the benefit to my will; receive salvation from my will." "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean." "I will; be clean." Is there no limit to the heretics' impiety? Do you see that in word he is subject, but by his own will he acts with authority?

When I say this, I am not presenting the Son's will as cut off from the Father's will. For whatever you call the Son's wish, you are calling the Father's wish; whatever you call the Father's wish, you are proclaiming the Son's authority; and if you speak of the Son's authority, you are pointing to the power of the Holy Spirit. For the power is one, and the kingdom is undivided. "But you passed over the question of the Spirit," he says. "From the apostle's words I find that the Spirit is subjected to Christ. For Paul said: 'But when it says that all things have been subjected to him, it is clear that he is excepted who subjected all things to him.' If only he who subjected them is excepted, is not the Spirit subjected? For he said that only the Father is not subjected to Christ." The words "all things" refer to creation; they do not insult the uncreated nature. He is speaking about the subjection of enemies: "The last enemy to be destroyed is death." Why, then, do you put the Holy Spirit in the place of the subjected enemies? Did the Father bring in a subjection of friends? Did he mention a subjection of angels? Did he touch on a subjection of archangels? It was a subjection of enemies: "The last enemy to be destroyed is death." The Holy Spirit is not among the subjected enemies. If we, the faithful who believe in Christ, will reign with him, will the Holy Spirit not even attain the same dignity as us, his subjects? At the Savior's appearing the sons of Zebedee, James and John, and the whole choir of the apostles will sit on twelve thrones, and will the Spirit be down at the footstool with the subjected? Turn away from impiety. The passage, man, is about creation, not about the uncreated nature, not about the dignity that is worshiped.

To receive an exact and carefully examined account of true piety, consider how blessed David, bringing in the choir of creation singing praise, says: "Praise the Lord from the heavens, praise him in the heights," and so on: angels, powers, the heavens of heavens, and the waters above the heavens. Did he mention the Spirit? Did he count the uncreated nature along with creation? The three youths with Ananias in the furnace also brought in the choir of creation, saying: "Sing praise, angels of the Lord, heavens of the Lord, powers of the Lord, sun and moon," and so on. Did they mention the Holy Spirit? Did they count the Uncreated along with creation? Paul again, distinguishing the invisible from the visible, says somewhere in his teaching: "For in Christ all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible," and at once he lists the invisible, saying: "whether thrones or principalities or authorities or dominions." All visible things are acknowledged to be in servitude. But the invisible include angels and powers, and also the Holy Spirit, the Son and the Father. So that you would not, through ignorance of how heaven is ordered, drag the lordly dignity of the divine Spirit under the yoke of slavery, he does not list the visible things one by one, or say, "whether sun or moon or stars, all are servants." Their status is acknowledged: "all things are your servants." But since principalities and angels were among the invisible, and the Spirit who is worshiped was also invisible, he lists everything above, lest anyone include the Spirit among the invisible things. He does so to exclude the Lord from the rank of servants. He lists those who worship, to set apart the One who is worshiped: "whether thrones or principalities or authorities." He did not say, "or the Spirit."

But let us come to our subject. "If you will, Lord, you can make me clean." The leper saw benefits gushing forth, saw salvation welling up, saw many who were sick and possessed by demons crowding around the fountain of salvation, and he laid aside all division of mind. He was leprous in body but clean in soul, for his soul was not divided into different colors. Leprosy is repulsive in the body because it divides the color of the skin; so a double heart, divided between faith and unbelief, is repulsive in the soul. As much revulsion as leprosy causes to the sight of human eyes, so much revulsion does a divided soul cause to the eyes of God. That is why Scripture says: "Woe to the double heart and the slack soul, and to the sinner who walks on two paths." But let us hold to our subject again. "I will; be clean." What a wonder! "I will; be clean." There is a word, brothers, that is often spoken out of authority, but often also out of boastfulness. Anyone at all can utter it, but only one who has the power can make the deed follow the claim of authority. If he had said "I will" and the deed had not followed, it would have been boastfulness. But in fact the deed followed the voice. If the word does not move you to respect, stand in awe of the deed.

See how great the difference is between the old law and the new grace in every respect. When Moses came down from the mountain, his first legislation and first law ordered that lepers be put out of the camp; when Christ came down from the mountain, he at once cleansed a leper. The one banishes the afflicted, the other heals their afflictions. Christ went up a mountain, and Moses went up one too: Moses to receive the law, Christ to give it. Moses went up and found the mountain filled with trumpets, cloud, thunder, lightning, storm and darkness. This was not because such things were fitting to the glory of the one who appeared, but because they trained the people in reverence. But the grace of Christ, brothers, sets fear aside and drives out slavery. For we did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear; we received a spirit of adoption. Moses gave ten commandments, but Jesus, Moses' Lord, gave nine beatitudes. Those who know the Scriptures know that what I say is true. The first beatitude: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted. Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled. Blessed are the merciful, for they will receive mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God. Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when people revile you and persecute you and falsely say every kind of evil against you."

Why, then, does the law have ten commandments, while grace has nine beatitudes? The number of the ten commandments equals the number of the plagues against the Egyptians: ten plagues against the Egyptians to chasten their arrogance, ten commandments for the people to correct their dullness. And the very letter, brothers, with which the number ten is written, the iota, I mean, has the shape and form of a rod. For it was a rod that disciplined both the Egyptians and the people. But Jesus our Lord gives nine beatitudes, weaving the crown of beatitudes three strands thick out of a threefold triad. For, brothers, since the worshipful Trinity, the royal dignity, the undefiled nature, the lordship that has no lord above it, has its glory in a triad, God honors on earth both the proclamation and the number of the virtues whenever that number matches the Holy Trinity. Here is what I mean. There were many patriarchs, yet God calls himself the God of the patriarchs in this way: "I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob." This is not because he was not the God of Moses, or not the God of Joseph, for he is the God of all who call on him in truth. Rather, he honors heavenly things in earthly ones, as in an image. Three patriarchs in honor of the Trinity; three virtues in honor of the Trinity: "And now these three remain: faith, hope, love." Creation is divided into three: the ranks of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth. Time is cut into three: past, present and future. And just as there were many patriarchs, yet a triad sufficed for the glorification of the Spirit, so too, though there were many priests, a triad of priests is singled out: "Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel." There were many kings and many priests, yet three are remembered: "Except for David, Hezekiah and Josiah," says the Scripture, "all sinned." In the furnace there were three youths; with Christ on the mountain were Peter, James and John. There are many angels in heaven, yet three appear to Abraham. All days belong to God, yet three serve the mystery of Christ. Which three? "Take Isaac, your only son, whom you love, and go to one of the mountains." And Abraham journeyed three days and three nights, so as to show the mystery at the same time. For he received Isaac back alive, as it were, from death. Hear how. From the moment Isaac was taken to be sacrificed, he was dead to his father; for it is not the outcome of the deed but the intention that makes the offering binding. As far as the intention went, Isaac had been put to death for his father; on the third day he was given back alive, as a figure of the resurrection. Jonah too could have spent many days in the sea, but he spends only three, to show the mystery of the resurrection.

"Then," someone says, "if you happen to find testimonies like these scattered here and there, do you take them up again as images of the Trinity and of the divine plan?" You do not want these signs? If I am the one saying it, reject the argument; but if the proclamation is divine, hear it from me. Better still, listen together with me, and learn that the three days signify the Lord's passion. For the Savior himself says of Abraham: "Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad." What day? The day of his death. For the ram given to Abraham from the tree bore the image of the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. To say "he saw the day" means nothing other than "he saw the death." How do we know this? We ourselves often say of people, "His day has come," meaning his end. But the rule of common usage is not enough to establish the point. What then? Let us turn to Scripture. Blessed David says somewhere: "The sinner will watch the righteous man and gnash his teeth at him; but the Lord will laugh at him, for he foresees that his day will come." So much, then, for Abraham. Now I will return to Jonah. For again, Jonah's three days signify the saving passion. Once more the Savior himself proclaims it: "Just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so the Son of Man must spend three days and three nights in the heart of the earth." But in addition to what has been said, let me give one proof stronger than the rest. The former people had three orders: priesthood, kingship and prophecy. Apart from these three offices, no other office was to be seen among the Jews: kingship, priesthood, prophecy. There was a horn of oil, the oil of sanctification. The anointing was one, but the gifts were three; the horn was one, but the graces were three. For with it they anointed priests, kings and prophets. But since some do not know the matter, and so that my words may not run on in vain, wearing themselves out while doing the listener no good, hear it briefly. There was a horn kept by the prophets. From that horn kings, prophets and priests were anointed. The ointment was not changed; rather, grace was given through the same horn, and so kings were anointed, priests were anointed, prophets were anointed: one anointing, three gifts. Why was the ointment kept in a horn? Because it bore the image of Christ. Could it not have been in a silver vessel? Could it not have been in a gold one? Could so great a gift not have been kept in some other, more precious material? It could, but it was not; it was kept in a horn, because, as I said before, it bore the image of Christ. For it is written: "I will make a horn sprout for David." May the Lord of priesthood, kingship and prophecy be with you all.
For once the chapter about the three men who were crushed into the horn had begun, he stopped.
